summary: This Center for Sustainable Systems publication compares life cycle environmental impacts of five dinner recipes sourced as meal kits versus grocery store meals, covering climate change, acidification, eutrophication, land use and water use. Inventory data came from direct measurement supplemented with literature, and a Monte Carlo analysis tested robustness. Grocery meals showed about 33% higher greenhouse gas emissions on average, with meal kits' supply chain, food waste and last-mile advantages outweighing their extra packaging.
one_line: Study finding meal kits have roughly 33% lower greenhouse gas emissions per meal than grocery store meals, due to supply chain, food waste and transport advantages.
key_facts: The study was published as CSS19-23 with a full publication date of August 2019.
Five dinner recipes were compared, sourced both as meal kits and through grocery store retailing.
Average grocery meal greenhouse gas emissions were 33% higher than meal kits, at 8.1 kg CO2e/meal compared with 6.1 kg CO2e/meal kit.
A Monte Carlo analysis found higher median emissions for grocery meals than meal kits for four out of five meals.
Grocery meal emissions were higher in 100% of model runs for two of the five meals.
Meal kits' streamlined, direct-to-consumer supply chains reduced emissions by 1.05 kg CO2e/meal.
Reduced food waste with meal kits lowered emissions by 0.86 kg CO2e/meal.
Lower last-mile transportation emissions for meal kits amounted to a reduction of 0.45 kg CO2e/meal.
Increased packaging for meal kits added 0.17 kg CO2e/meal in emissions.
Meal kit refrigeration packs present an average emissions decrease of 0.37 kg CO2e/meal compared with retail refrigeration.
Meals with the largest environmental impact either contain red meat or are associated with large amounts of wasted food.
The one meal kit with higher emissions is due to food mass differences rather than supply chain logistics.
The paper was authored by Brent R. Heard, Mayur Bandekar, Benjamin Vassar and Shelie A. Miller, and published in Resources, Conservation and Recycling 147: 189-200.
The study's digital object identifier is https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2019.04.008.
